intro: Rachmaninoff recorded his Prelude in C♯ minor, Op. 3 No. 2, the encore he played most often, for Victor in 1921. The prelude opens with three low notes, and its later chords are so broad that the score is written on four staves.

sections.label: A · A–G♯–C♯ motif, then triplets
sections.mNote: A–G♯–C♯ sounds in the bass beneath quiet chords.

sections.label: B · Agitato in triplets
sections.mNote: The Agitato melody rises over running notes.

sections.label: C · Opening chords return
sections.mNote: The chords are written across four staves.

sections.label: D · Closing chords over low C♯

cues.title: Opening three-note motif
cues.text: The piece opens with A–G♯–C♯ played in octaves, fortissimo. The chords that follow are marked ppp. The same three-note descent repeats in the bass beneath the chords.
cues.evidence: Bosworth (1896) and Universal Edition (1910), opening upbeat and bars 1–4; Petro Kostandy’s Mutopia engraving. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Agitato, bars 14–17
cues.text: In the Agitato, triplet quavers surround a melody that descends E–D♯–D♮–C♯. The right hand plays both parts, with the melody in its upper notes and the triplets below.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 14–17: Agitato, with the descending melody separately stemmed above triplet quavers. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Composition and demand as an encore
cues.text: Rachmaninoff wrote the Prelude at nineteen. Years later, audiences still demanded it as an encore before letting him leave the platform, in recital halls around the world.
cues.evidence: Robert Matthew-Walker, notes to Hyperion CDA66081, on the Prelude’s composition and persistent demand as an encore. The issued take of this 1921 Victor transfer remains unidentified. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W6690_66081

cues.title: Return of the opening chords
cues.text: The opening chords return at Tempo primo, now marked fff pesante, very loud and heavy. Rachmaninoff writes this passage on four staves, two for each hand, and the bell figure spreads across the whole keyboard.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 45–48: Tempo primo, fff pesante and four-stave piano notation. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Closing chords over low C♯
cues.text: A low C♯ is held beneath the last sequence of chords. Above it the hands move by small steps, and the final C♯ minor chord is held under a fermata, ppp.
cues.evidence: Bosworth and Universal Edition score, bars 55–61: sustained low C♯ and the final ppp chord with fermata. https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=2033
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition
Ivanovka, Dresden, New York, Villa Senar and Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
